skills.name: Guided work: checking a square-of-opposition record

note.text: Work with an invented finite class on paper or on this screen. Separate S members inside P from S members outside P and state that these counts cover all S. Record A, E, I and O by their definitions before consulting the square. A mixed class supplies useful counterexamples to false upward inferences. An empty class tests whether existence was silently assumed. These are logical models, not a survey of actual pupils.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to construct a complete counted model and use it to detect an unjustified square inference. Builds on: square relations and existence conditions. Leads to: conversion, obversion and checking transformations.

sections.heading: Understand the pattern
sections.text: Work with an invented finite class on paper or on this screen. Separate S members inside P from S members outside P and state that these counts cover all S. Record A, E, I and O by their definitions before consulting the square. A mixed class supplies useful counterexamples to false upward inferences. An empty class tests whether existence was silently assumed. These are logical models, not a survey of actual pupils.

sections.heading: Read the original model
sections.text: Original record: {3} S are P and {2} S are not P; no other S exist. I and O are true because each region contains members. A and E are false because each has a counterexample. A pupil’s claim that I true forces A true fails in this same model. Next change the outside count to {0}: now A is true, while the remaining inside count keeps I true.

sections.heading: Apply and check
sections.text: Prepare columns for inside/outside counts and the truth of A/E/I/O. Try a mixed, all-inside, all-outside and empty model. Compare a proposed inference with each record; a true premise and false conclusion gives a counterexample.

worked_example.problem: Test I true therefore A true using {3} S inside P and {2} outside P.
steps: The inside count {3} makes I true.
The outside count {2} supplies a counterexample to A.
So the premise is true and conclusion false in this complete model.

cards.idea: Distinguish the ideas used in this lesson.
example: complete record: counts covering every S in the invented model.
mixed model: existing S both inside and outside P.
counterexample model: a model with a true premise and false proposed conclusion.
recorded assumption: an explicit condition governing a model’s use.

cards.idea: Read the whole example before identifying its function.
example: The model states there are no other S.
Positive counts in both regions make I and O true.
I true with A false refutes an unrestricted I-to-A inference.
Mark whether S exists before applying the full square.

cards.idea: A correction must preserve scope, terms and assumptions.
example: Unreported S can be added while still calling the supplied model complete. Correction: Completeness fixes the whole subject class.
A mixed model makes A true. Correction: An outside member refutes A.
A false premise and true conclusion alone refute validity. Correction: Invalidity needs premises true and conclusion false.
An existence condition may be omitted without affecting every inference. Correction: Some square directions depend on existence.

questions.correct: {(X.code=="A" ? b==0 : X.code=="E" ? a==0 : X.code=="I" ? a>0 : b>0) ? "True in this model." : "False in this model."}

misconceptions.explain: That reverses the result of checking the relevant region.
Both S regions and completeness are supplied, so this claim can be assessed.
Some asserts existence, not an exact total; the supplied counts still determine truth.

solution: Some means at least one. A has no S outside P; E has no S inside P.
Here A is {b==0}, E is {a==0}, I is {a>0} and O is {b>0}.
